terms.grammar: pronoun: genitive ejus, dative eī; plural eī (iī), eae, ea
evidence: Liv. 40.21.2: cupīdō eum cēperat in verticem Haemī montis ascendendī
Cic. Tusc. 5.108: cujātem sē esse dīceret
terms.comment: The plain “he” of narration and talk, unstressed: cupīdō eum cēperat, a longing had taken hold of him. As subject it is mostly left out, the verb’s ending being enough (tum sē quiētī dedit, then he went to bed). In reported speech and wishes, “he” meaning the speaker is the reflexive sē (see himself): cujātem sē esse dīceret, where he would say he was from.

evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: ut illum amēs
terms.comment: For a person spoken of with some weight, or to turn to a new subject in a story (ille: nē istud dīxerīs, and he said, “Don’t say that”). Beside hic, ille is the former and hic the latter.
The man present or just named: “this one here”.

terms.gloss: he, that man (near you; often with scorn)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.4.3: Cicerō meus quid aget? iste vērō sit in sinū semper et complexū meō
terms.comment: The one beside the person spoken to: Cicero, writing to his wife, calls the little boy who is with her iste. In speeches it is often scornful, “that fellow”.

phrases.latin: cupīdō eum cēperat in verticem Haemī montis ascendendī
phrases.english: A longing had taken hold of him to climb to the top of Mount Haemus.

phrases.latin: tum sē quiētī dedit et quiēvit vērissimō quidem somnō
phrases.english: Then he went to bed, and slept a truly sound sleep.

phrases.latin: Sōcratēs quidem cum rogārētur cujātem sē esse dīceret, 'mundānum' inquit
phrases.english: When Socrates was asked what country he would say he was from, he said, “The world.”

phrases.latin: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
phrases.english: For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do myself.

phrases.latin: Cicerō meus quid aget? iste vērō sit in sinū semper et complexū meō
phrases.english: And how will my little Cicero be? Let him always be in your lap and your arms.

phrases.latin: caput eum ad fornicem Fabium offendisse
phrases.english: that he had bumped his head on the Arch of Fabius

hic.against: Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel
hic.html: De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke. Likewise the neuter hoc (hocc), against the ablative hōc.

sources: Lewis & Short: is · Lewis & Short: ille · Lewis & Short: hic · Lewis & Short: iste
